arc: The teaching unfolds the inmost Divine — the First Father of Greatness — by naming the five faculties and twelve Wisdoms in which he stands established, then traces how five great attributes gush forth from him into all the aeons, sealing and nourishing every state and making them live forever.
title: The First Father and the Five Attributes that Gush Forth into the Aeons
reading:
This chapter is a portrait of the inmost Divine in his own substance and in the way he proceeds. It opens with a promise that pertains to everything that follows: the light shall be poured upon those who hear, and they shall recognize him. The whole teaching is then that recognition — a description of the Father of Greatness as the unmeasured source from which all love and wisdom proceed, displayed first in his interior structure and then in the attributes by which he flows into the aeons.

The Father is shown as one who simply is — "the one who exists" — and who is established in his five members of light. These five members are the discrete degrees of the Divine itself considered as receptive form: the mind, the thought, the teaching, the counsel, and (lost in the lacuna) the reflection — the five intellectual faculties that in the human are receptacles, but in the Father are his own inmost articulation of love-and-wisdom in form. The teaching insists that these members "have no measure nor measure-rule"; that is, although they are an ordered fivefold structure, in the Father they are the unmeasured fullness of which every measured five elsewhere in the cosmos is only a faint correspondence. Above this fivefold the teaching names twelve members of light, and these twelve are identified as the twelve Wisdoms — the complete articulation of Divine Wisdom in the fullness of its aspects, the celestial counterpart of every twelvefold ordering that will appear lower down (the twelve Hours, the zodiac, the apostolic completeness). Five and twelve together give the inmost Divine first as discrete degrees of faculty and then as the full church of wisdoms in which those faculties express themselves.

From this established interior the teaching moves to procession. Out of each of the five great members five attributes "gush forth," and these are given in sequence. The first is his Light, which streams from him in oneness throughout all the aeons — Divine Truth in its illuminating quality, the substance of the Father's land radiating outward without losing its unity. The second is his Fragrance, spreading into all the aeons of the Greatness — the diffusing presence of Divine Love, the perceived sweetness of conjunction by which the Father is felt wherever he is present. The third is his beautiful Voice, sounding through all the aeons — Divine Truth as Word, the proceeding speech that orders and calls. The fourth and fifth are largely lost to the lacunae, but the pattern is clear: each is another mode by which the inmost Divine pours himself outward, gushing forth into all the aeons as light, fragrance, voice, and the remaining two qualities of glory.

The latter half of the teaching describes what these five attributes do once they have gone forth. They are revealed outward, they seal in those who receive them, and they are sent forth so that the aeons themselves are nourished. The seal is the imprint of confirmed correspondence: where the attribute touches a receptive state it stamps upon it the character of the Father, fixing the conjunction. The nourishing is the continuous influx by which heavenly states have their life. What gushes forth from the Mother — the matrix of divine generation — is then said to make the aeons new, so that they grow rich in the ordering, beautiful in their order, and live unto eternity. Procession from the Father, sealing in the receptive, nourishment of the aeons, and renewal in the bringing-forth of the Mother are one continuous act, and that act is what makes a state "living" in the strict sense — conjoined with the Lord and therefore unending.

The spiritual argument of the chapter is therefore this: the Lord in his inmost Divine is not a bare unity but an ordered fullness — five faculties and twelve Wisdoms — and from that fullness he proceeds into every level of heaven by five distinct qualities (light, fragrance, voice, and two more), each of which carries his whole being into the receptive state, seals it, feeds it, and renews it forever. Every later teaching in the corpus about five faculties in the soul, five Sons of the First Man, five Storehouses, and the twelvefold ordering of the heavens depends on this: those lower fives and twelves are correspondential reflections of the Father's own five members and twelve Wisdoms, and the life that runs in them is nothing other than these gushing-forth attributes received in their measure.
